name: Finn
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The passage set under Finn actually gathers several figures named Eochaid. One of them, Eochaid Finn Emna, had a brother, Eochaid Airem, and the two may be the same man, for both are said to have married Étain. Another, Eochaid Iúil, rules the Otherworld and is sometimes named husband of the fairy queen Fand. Next, Eochaid mac Eirc wed the goddess Tailtiu and stands among the ideal kings of legend. In his day the land gave fruit, the rain fell gentle as dew, and no one lied. A member of the Fir Bolg, an old race, he resisted the magic-wielding Tuatha Dé Danann when they came and died at the first conflict on Mag Tuired. Eochaid Garbh, Tailtiu's second husband, may have set up the Lughnasa gathering at Teltown. Eochaid Mugmedón, a king from the edge of history, is named the father of Niall, lord of the Nine Hostages, an ancestor from whom many ruling lines claimed descent. Eochaid Ollathair, meaning all-father, serves as a name for the great Dagda.
